Minor coastal flooding possible.

Models continue to stay in general agreement with the development of 
a low pressure system off the southeast coast this weekend, later 
phasing with a mid-level trough over the northeast. This will 
support the a deepening coastal low tracking northward toward 
southern New England. Within this amplified flow, a plume of above 
normal moisture, 290-330 percent of normal, surges northward ahead 
of the approaching trough and coastal low. This will prime the 
environment for heavy rainfall once the better forcing/instability 
arrive with the low. Models have also come into better agreement 
with the track of the low which should likely track across or near 
the Cape and Islands overnight Sunday into early Monday. There are 
subtle differences in track that could shift the axis of 
heavier rainfall east or west as a result.

Model guidance continues to highlight this system as fairly 
progressive with rain arriving later Sunday and out by mid-morning 
Monday. Despite it being quick moving, the environment favors it to 
drop a good amount of rain in a short period. Deterministic and 
ensemble guidance show swath of 1-3" across southern New 
England. Overall, we are still seeing variance how far west or 
east of this swatch will be. This is likely a result of the 
variance in low track and its frontal features with the heavier 
rain amounts/rates being favored in proximity to the stronger 
forcing and instability. Overall we can likely expect widespread
rain, heavy at times, although there is still uncertainty in 
where the heavier localized bands will set up. Given the 
progressive nature of the system, flash flood risk is low, 
although can't rule out ponding of water or urban/poor drainage 
flooding. 

Gusty winds will also accompany the low supported by a strong 
pressure gradient with a 50-60 kt southerly LLJ positioned near the 
Cape/Islands. The magnitude of the gusts will depend on the finer 
details such as the track/strength of the low. A closer(more 
west) track will position strong gusts across the coastal 
waters, Cape and Islands, and potentially parts of the south 
coast. Given that majority of this occurs overnight, a nighttime
inversion should limit the full degree of mixing of the 50-60 
kt gusts to the surface. Gusts likely range 25-45 mph with the 
strongest winds/gusts near the Cape and Islands. Ensembles 
generally show probabilities of 40-70% for gusts 40mph or 
greater for Cape/Islands and low probabilities along the 
immediate south coast/SE MA. Strong gusts likely diminish 
throughout Monday morning. 

Despite the rising astronomical tides, the quick moving system 
shouldn't bring major coastal flooding impacts. Splashover to very 
minor coastal flooding is possible for the Mon high tide along the 
east coast, Cape, and Nantucket. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Potential for an impactful Nor'easter Wed night into 
Thanksgiving. Mainly rain is expected but some snow/ice is possible, 
especially across the high elevations of the interior. Strong winds 
with dangerous marine conditions are likely and coastal flooding is 
possible. 

A much colder post-frontal airmass settles over SNE on Tuesday and 
Wednesday under building high pressure...925 mb temps drop from
~10C on Monday to -3C Tue/Wed. While we'll see plenty of sun 
each day highs will still only make it into the 40s. The change 
is also drastic when it comes to low temperatures if you compare
the expected lows of mid to upper 50s Sunday night to teens and
20s Tuesday night aided by radiational cooling. 

The respite from the wet weather will only last a few days as global 
guidance continues to have good consensus in our next in a 
series of coastal storms arriving late Wednesday or Thursday. 
This, as we see a negatively tilted trough digging into the 
southeast U.S. Wednesday and lifting across New England late 
week. In the mid levels two distinct pieces of energy in the 
northern and southern stream will be close to phasing but at the
moment look to remain distinct. Strengthening surface low 
pressure will be running up against a high over the Canadian 
maritimes making for a tight pressure gradient and very strong 
winds. While there is good agreement that we will be dealing 
with a strong storm (stronger than the weekend storm), there is 
still significant uncertainty with regard to the exact track and
timing (i.e. does it arrive Wednesday night or Thanksgiving 
day?). This track and timing will be crucial not just for 
knowing when to expect the strongest winds and heavy rain, but 
whether or not the peak winds align with high tides. Tides will 
be astronomically high, so coastal flooding has potential to be
